q: Is it leakage if my replaced boiler or motor is sold and used elsewhere?
title: Leakage when old equipment is reused
short: Usually yes. If the boiler or motor you replaced keeps running somewhere else, carbon methods treat that as leakage, because its emissions have moved rather than stopped. Most small-scale methods expect the old unit to be scrapped with evidence, or the transfer to be counted and deducted from your credits.
audience: Indian factories planning energy efficiency or fuel switch credits

p: An efficiency or fuel switch credit pays for emissions that no longer happen. If your inefficient boiler is sold to another unit and fired there, the emissions you claimed to avoid partly continue, outside your project boundary. That shift is leakage. Verra's VCS Standard requires leakage to be assessed and deducted, and CDM small-scale methods for equipment replacement handle it by requiring the old equipment to be taken out of use.

sections.h: What counts as taking it out of use
ul: Scrapped and destroyed: cut up and sold as metal scrap. This is not leakage.
Kept on site as cold standby, sealed and logged, with no running hours. Allowed in some methods, but expect the verifier to check meters and fuel records.
Sold or transferred as working equipment to another factory: leakage, unless the method lets you show it replaces an even less efficient unit there, which is hard to prove.
Moved to another line in your own plant: it stays inside your boundary only if that line is in the project; otherwise treat it as leakage.

sections.h: How remaining lifetime affects the claim
p: CDM Methodological Tool 10 sets how to estimate the remaining lifetime of the equipment you replace. Reductions are credited against the old equipment only until it would have reached the end of its life anyway. Equipment near the end of its life gives a short crediting window, which is one more reason to document its age, rating and condition before removal.

sections.h: Evidence to keep for the verifier
ol: Make, model, serial number and nameplate rating of each replaced unit, with photos.
A scrap sale invoice or scrap dealer certificate naming the equipment, and a weighbridge slip.
Photos of the unit being cut or dismantled, dated.
The purchase invoice and commissioning report of the new equipment.
A written statement from your side that no replaced unit was sold for reuse.

senseible: Senseible shows carbon credit eligibility signals and keeps the purchase and scrap invoices you upload as evidence. It does not calculate leakage deductions or decide methodology compliance; that sits with the project developer, the verifier and the registry.

sources.label: CDM Methodological Tool 10, remaining lifetime of equipment, and small-scale methodologies AMS-II.C and AMS-II.D (UNFCCC)

reviewNote: CDM methods are being carried into the Article 6.4 mechanism; check the version of the methodology your project registers under.
